narrative: Statutory civil remedy under PC § 290.46(j)(4)(A): actual damages or $25,000, whichever is greater, plus attorney fees, for each unlawful use of registry information. CONSERVATIVE: ~$45,000 (statutory minimum plus modest emotional distress; Plaintiff was re-onboarded but had not yet commenced active paid shifts before the anticipated adverse action, so lost-wage recovery tracks the failure-to-hire posture of Matters 25 and 26 unless wages were actually earned during the July 7–adverse-action window). MODERATE: ~$110,000 (statutory penalty; ICRAA statutory plus punitive for willful noncompliance; emotional distress; fee-shifting under §290.46(j)(4)(A); if even one paid shift was worked, Tameny wrongful-termination damages add a meaningful lost-wages increment at CDL commercial-driving rates). AGGRESSIVE: ~$250,000 (aggregation across all six causes of action; punitive damages under Civ. Code §3294 multiplied by the portfolio-wide pattern of violations across five separate employers; if the CDL placement was operative and Plaintiff worked shifts, ongoing lost wage loss at CDL rates adds significantly; RK Logistics named as co-defendant adds end-client liability and creates cross-pressure between Randstad and RK Logistics, each incentivized to attribute the placement decision to the other).
risk: Extremely favorable — this is no longer an information-and-belief case. Plaintiff holds the actual InfoMart background check report (Order No. 15780719). The report conclusively shows: (1) every criminal court search (7 county/state jurisdictions) returned 'No Record'; federal criminal, OFAC, OIG, and GSA all clear; (2) the one and only flagged item is the National Sex Offender Search result — 'Subject is a registered Sex Offender in California'; (3) the overall report status is 'NEEDS APPROVAL, PER CLIENT CRITERIA' — not a flat rejection by InfoMart, but a flag sent to RK Logistics for its decision. This places the adverse decision squarely with RK Logistics and Randstad. The InfoMart report header makes RK Logistics' role undeniable: Billing Code 'RK LOGISTICS,' Business Unit 'RIS RK Logistics Fremont,' Client Package 'RK Logistics' — RK Logistics configured the screening criteria that triggered the 'NEEDS APPROVAL' flag. PC §290.46(j)(2)(E) is a categorical prohibition applicable to all employment purposes regardless of position or employer type; no 'protect a person at risk' exception could plausibly apply to a CDL commercial truck-driving placement. The InfoMart report itself contains the required California ICRA notice (Civ. Code §1786.26) and the FCRA Summary of Rights — confirming that InfoMart and Randstad/RK Logistics are on notice of the statutory framework. The two-defendant structure (Randstad as employer of record + RK Logistics as the criteria-setting end client) creates joint-and-several liability and cross-defendant settlement pressure: each party will be incentivized to attribute the adverse action decision to the other, potentially generating additional admissions. No qualified immunity available (state law, private employers). This matter is now evidentiary comparably to Matter 22 (Pilot), where the post-adverse action notice was the smoking gun — here the BGC report itself serves that role because it proves the registry hit and that every other search was clear. On July 21, 2026, RK Logistics responded to the pre-filing demand denying liability on two grounds. The first — that Randstad, not RK Logistics, was Plaintiff's employer — threatens only the Tameny wrongful-termination claim, which requires an employer-employee relationship; it does not reach the other five causes of action, none of which turn on formal employer status the same way. It is also in tension with RK Logistics' own Transportation Manager, Jack Altares, who wrote on July 15, 2026 that 'Brendan's MVR came back and unfortunately, we will not be able to move forward with him as a driver for RK' — RK Logistics personnel making the substantive placement decision, cutting against the letter's claim that RK Logistics 'did not and could not' act as an employer. The second ground — that the rejection was MVR-based, not registry-based — initially appeared serious: RK Logistics attached a SambaSafety report showing a commercial (Class A) disqualification for refusing a CMV chemical test (eff. 12/1/2024) and a related suspension (eff. 2/20/2025, cleared 5/19/2026). On review, both entries attach to Plaintiff's commercial driving privileges, not the non-commercial Class C license the RK Logistics 'Class C Driver' posting required; Plaintiff holds documentation of a Class C license reissue dated June 11, 2026 — three weeks after the suspension cleared and five weeks before he applied to RK Logistics — which the SambaSafety report's own 'PENDING APPLICATION' notation is consistent with. As between the two named defendants, Randstad's exposure remains the more direct and is not reduced by RK Logistics' response: Randstad ordered the InfoMart background check, received the pre-adverse notice, and delivered the July 15 termination — two business days after the pre-adverse notice, short of FCRA's five-business-day waiting period — and has no employer-status defense available to it at all. Randstad's Aug. 18, 2026 move — retaining outside employment-defense counsel who asked for an opening demand before serving any responsive pleading or meet-and-confer letter — reads as pricing the case rather than testing it. The demand's shape matters: a global number lets the two defendants allocate between themselves and settles away the cross-defendant pressure a Randstad-only number preserves.
